title: JPMorgan Sticks With Chip-Equipment Leaders as AI Buildout Drives Tool Demand
excerpt: JPMorgan stays Overweight on Applied Materials, KLA and Lam Research — and Friday’s SOX action showed investors agree: chip-making tools are Wall Street’s preferred AI-buildout bet.
body:
• JPMorgan remains Overweight on Applied Materials, KLA and Lam Research — its three large-cap semiconductor equipment picks — with KLA the firm’s top semicap pick, described as a “picks-and-shovels play on advanced chip manufacturing.”
  • The firm raised its Applied Materials price target to $660 from $515 in August 2026.
  • On Friday, chip-gear makers Lam Research, Applied Materials and KLA were among the top SOX performers as the index broke above its 50-day moving average, with investors favoring manufacturing tools amid expectations for sustained AI-related capacity expansion, according to Investor’s Business Daily.
  • JPMorgan’s equipment thesis: wafer-fab equipment spending growing 5–7%, with large-cap equipment names outgrowing WFE by 300–700 basis points through manufacturing complexity, share gains, SAM expansion and resilient services businesses.

The AI buildout’s most durable trade may be the tools that make the chips. JPMorgan’s semiconductor analysts continue to back the chip-equipment complex, holding Overweight ratings on Applied Materials, KLA and Lam Research — the three large-cap wafer-fab equipment names — with KLA as the firm’s top semicap pick.

The market is listening. On Friday, Lam Research, Applied Materials and KLA were among the top performers in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index as the SOX broke above its 50-day moving average, Investor’s Business Daily reported — investors “favoring semiconductor manufacturing tools amid expectations for sustained AI-related capacity expansion.”

“Fears of an AI bubble are likely here to stay. But a strong spending landscape means many semiconductor stocks can still thrive.”

— Harlan Sur, semiconductor analyst, JPMorgan (via Morningstar)

The equipment thesis

JPMorgan’s case for the toolmakers rests on manufacturing complexity. In its 3Q preview thesis, the firm sees wafer-fab equipment spending growing 5–7%, with the large-cap equipment names outgrowing that rate by 300–700 basis points — through greater process complexity, share gains, served-market expansion and resilient services businesses. Data-center capex, analyst Harlan Sur has argued, could “rise another 50% next year, after surging an estimated 65% in 2025.”

The firm’s conviction extends beyond the equipment names: its broader semiconductor top picks have included Broadcom, Marvell, Micron, Analog Devices and Microchip (chips), Synopsys (EDA), and an Overweight on Nvidia. In August 2026, JPMorgan raised its Applied Materials price target to $660 from $515, per ainvest’s reporting.

A corroborating call from BofA

The equipment thesis got a powerful corroboration this week from Bank of America, whose semiconductor analysts forecast wafer-fabrication equipment spending more than doubling — from $155.9 billion in 2026 to $359.8 billion by 2030 — as the global chip market nearly doubles to $3.2 trillion. BofA’s preferred equipment names overlap JPMorgan’s: Lam Research and Applied Materials, both Buy-rated.

What to watch

The overhang on the trade is well known: BofA’s June 2026 fund manager survey found a record 80% of 198 managers, overseeing $540 billion, calling long-semiconductors the most crowded trade — the “fear of heights” sentiment coexisting with the bullish forecasts. The biggest risk both firms flag is a slowdown in hyperscaler AI spending.

For portfolio investors, the message from Wall Street’s two biggest semiconductor desks is consistent: bet on contracted capacity, not sentiment. The equipment names sit at the front of the AI supply chain — the picks and shovels — and both JPMorgan and BofA expect their order books to keep growing through the AI buildout.
nri_angle: For US-based Indian investors, Wall Street’s equipment-first AI thesis translates into a portfolio lens: the SOX’s equipment leaders are where JPMorgan and BofA see the most durable AI-buildout exposure.
author: Diaspora Desk
